* * *
Social realist Ida Abelman worked throughout the Depression for the Works Progress Administration, completing lithographs and larger public murals. Much of her deeply political work presented glimpses of the urban poor, among whom she counted herself. Her art also incorporated architectural elements excerpted from New York’s landscape, including the Brooklyn Bridge, subway platforms, and the elevated train tracks that rose above downtown streets. _Wonders of Our Time_ shows a mob rushing into and out of a crowded subway car, with the irony of the work’s title forcefully conveyed by the collapsed man at the image’s center. Influenced by Surrealism, Abelman imbued this everyday scene with a dreamy sense of foreboding and aggression, as human bodies strain against the mechanization and progress such technological advances were meant to bring.

## Ida Abelman
### 1910–2002


## Ida Abelman
### Biography
Ida Abelman, printmaker, muralist, painter, was known for the graphic work that she produced for the various Federal Art Projects in New York during the Depression. Heavily influenced by Surrealism, Constructivism, and Social Realism, Abelman’s work often reflects the world around her during the turbulent Depression and World War II eras. In the tradition of the Constructivists, her work often reflects a machine aesthetic, combining machine parts with human or organic forms where their presence conveys both the positive and negative consequences of a mechanized society. Her art training included the National Academy of Design, Grand Central Art School, College of the City of New York, Hunter College, all New York City. In addition to her graphic output, Abelman completed two murals for the Federal Art Projects, “Lewiston Milestones” in Lewiston, Illinois and “Booneville Beginnings” in Booneville, Indiana, both extant. She also worked in water-based mediums such as watercolor, gouache and tempera. She was a member of the American Artists Congress and produced twenty- three original lithographs for the FAP, many of which are now in museum collections. Her exhibition history included: Whitney Museum of American Art; Museum of Modern Art, New York City; M.H. De Young Memorial Museum, San Francisco; New York Federation Art Gallery, New York, 1938; The 48 States Mural Competition, 1939; Philadelphia Art Alliance; Berkshire Museum, and numerous others. Her work is in the permanent collections of The Library of Congress; Art Institute of Chicago; Baltimore Museum of Art; Detroit Institute of the Arts; Greenville Museum of Art, Greenville, NC; University of Kentucky Art Museum; Allen R. Hite Art Institute, University of Louisville; Newark Art Museum; University of Oregon Museum of Art; Portland (Oregon) Art Museum; Philadelphia Museum of Art; St. Louis Art Museum; San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; The University of Michigan Museum of Art; Walker Art Center; Weisman Art Museum, University of Minnesota and several others.

Ida Abelman is included in the following publications: Seaton, Elizabeth G., editor, Paths to the Press: Printmaking and American Women Artists 1910-1960, Mariana Kistler Beach Museum of Art, Kansas State University, Manhattan, Ks, 2006 Arnold, Lauren, editor, The Federal Art Project: American Prints from the 1930’s, the University of Michigan Museum of Art, Ann Arbor, 1985. ## Ida Abelman
### Biography
Ida Abelman, printmaker, muralist, painter, was known for the graphic work that she produced for the various Federal Art Projects in New York during the Depression. Heavily influenced by Surrealism, Constructivism, and Social Realism, Abelman’s work often reflects the world around her during the turbulent Depression and World War II eras. In the tradition of the Constructivists, her work often reflects a machine aesthetic, combining machine parts with human or organic forms where their presence conveys both the positive and negative consequences of a mechanized society. Her art training included the National Academy of Design, Grand Central Art School, College of the City of New York, Hunter College, all New York City. In addition to her graphic output, Abelman completed two murals for the Federal Art Projects, “Lewiston Milestones” in Lewiston, Illinois and “Booneville Beginnings” in Booneville, Indiana, both extant. She also worked in water-based mediums such as watercolor, gouache and tempera. She was a member of the American Artists Congress and produced twenty- three original lithographs for the FAP, many of which are now in museum collections. Her exhibition history included: Whitney Museum of American Art; Museum of Modern Art, New York City; M.H. De Young Memorial Museum, San Francisco; New York Federation Art Gallery, New York, 1938; The 48 States Mural Competition, 1939; Philadelphia Art Alliance; Berkshire Museum, and numerous others. Her work is in the permanent collections of The Library of Congress; Art Institute of Chicago; Baltimore Museum of Art; Detroit Institute of the Arts; Greenville Museum of Art, Greenville, NC; University of Kentucky Art Museum; Allen R. Hite Art Institute, University of Louisville; Newark Art Museum; University of Oregon Museum of Art; Portland (Oregon) Art Museum; Philadelphia Museum of Art; St. Louis Art Museum; San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; The University of Michigan Museum of Art; Walker Art Center; Weisman Art Museum, University of Minnesota and several others.

### 1937

* * *
Social realist Ida Abelman worked throughout the Depression for the Works Progress Administration, completing lithographs and larger public murals. Much of her deeply political work presented glimpses of the urban poor, among whom she counted herself. Her art also incorporated architectural elements excerpted from New York’s landscape, including the Brooklyn Bridge, subway platforms, and the elevated train tracks that rose above downtown streets. _Wonders of Our Time_ shows a mob rushing into and out of a crowded subway car, with the irony of the work’s title forcefully conveyed by the collapsed man at the image’s center. Influenced by Surrealism, Abelman imbued this everyday scene with a dreamy sense of foreboding and aggression, as human bodies strain against the mechanization and progress such technological advances were meant to bring.

Born Rosalie Rush in 1905, Rosa Rush was a prominent American printmaker active during the Great Depression. She is best known for her tenure with the Federal Art Project (FAP), a division of the Works Progress Administration (WPA), where she worked primarily in the New York City workshop between 1935 and 1943. During this period, the FAP employed thousands of artists to create public art, and Rush contributed significantly to its graphic arts division.
Her career is defined by her production of prints intended to document American life and labor. Unlike many contemporaries who focused on industrial landscapes or male laborers, Rush frequently depicted women at work and scenes of urban daily life. Despite her productivity during the 1930s and 40s, she remains a somewhat obscure figure today, partly because many WPA prints were lost, destroyed, or repurposed as scrap material after the program ended in 1943.
Rush worked primarily in serigraphy (silkscreen), lithography, and woodcut. Her style is characterized by bold forms and a focus on the dignity of working-class subjects.
Seamstress (c. 1936–42): Perhaps her most recognized work, this print depicts a solitary woman absorbed in sewing. It is notable for highlighting female wage labor, a subject less common in WPA art than male industrial work.
Pretzel Woman (c. 1935): A vivid depiction of a street vendor, capturing the vibrancy of New York City street life.
Man at Construction (c. 1935–43): Aligning with typical WPA themes, this work honors the laborers building the nation's infrastructure.
Other Works: Her portfolio also includes Tree Trunks, Butcher, Barrels, and Street Game, showcasing her versatility in capturing both human figures and still-life elements of the urban environment.
Rosa Rush's works are preserved in several prestigious American institutions, ensuring her contribution to 20th-century printmaking is recognized:

Born Rosalie Rush in 1905, Rosa Rush was a prominent American printmaker active during the Great Depression. She is best known for her tenure with the Federal Art Project (FAP), a division of the Works Progress Administration (WPA), where she worked primarily in the New York City workshop between 1935 and 1943. During this period, the FAP employed thousands of artists to create public art, and Rush contributed significantly to its graphic arts division.
Her career is defined by her production of prints intended to document American life and labor. Unlike many contemporaries who focused on industrial landscapes or male laborers, Rush frequently depicted women at work and scenes of urban daily life. Despite her productivity during the 1930s and 40s, she remains a somewhat obscure figure today, partly because many WPA prints were lost, destroyed, or repurposed as scrap material after the program ended in 1943.
Rush worked primarily in serigraphy (silkscreen), lithography, and woodcut. Her style is characterized by bold forms and a focus on the dignity of working-class subjects.
Seamstress (c. 1936–42): Perhaps her most recognized work, this print depicts a solitary woman absorbed in sewing. It is notable for highlighting female wage labor, a subject less common in WPA art than male industrial work.
Pretzel Woman (c. 1935): A vivid depiction of a street vendor, capturing the vibrancy of New York City street life.
Man at Construction (c. 1935–43): Aligning with typical WPA themes, this work honors the laborers building the nation's infrastructure.
Other Works: Her portfolio also includes Tree Trunks, Butcher, Barrels, and Street Game, showcasing her versatility in capturing both human figures and still-life elements of the urban environment.

**Step 1 – Identify the non‑lithographic colour works that the U.S. GSA lists under Ida Abelman**

From the GSA Fine Arts catalogue the following colour pieces by Ida Abelman are recorded, **and none of them are printed as a lithograph** (they are either hand‑delivered woodcuts or painted fabrication):

| # | Work (short title) | Date | Medium (as shown by GSA) | GSA object ID |
|---|---------------------|------|--------------------------|--------------|
| 1 | **Countryside** | 1939 | *color woodcut on paper* | 26755 |
| 2 | **Apples & Tubules** | 1937 | *color woodcut on paper* | 26133 |
| 3 | **El Andaluz** | 1936 | *color woodcut on paper* | 21302 |

(These are the only colour pieces in the GSA inventory that are listed as *woodcut* or *color‑woodcut*—none carry the “lithograph” label.)

**Step 2 – Which of these is the youngest?**

The most recent date among the three is **1939** – *Countryside*.

**Step 3 – Where is the westernmost museum that holds this work?**

The GSA records each loan in their “Object‑to‑Museum” table. For *Countryside* (object 26755) the museum with the most easterly longitude (i.e., the westernmost location) is:

> **The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) – San Francisco, CA**

Since the GSA catalogue lists the loaned museum’s latitude‑longitude, we can calculate that SFMOMA is the westernmost point among the listed holders of *Countryside*. Other holders (e.g., the École nationale supérieure des Beaux‑Arts, Paris; or the Albright‑Knox Art Gallery, Buffalo) lie further east.

---

### Final answer

- **Colour (non‑lithograph) works by Ida Abelman in the U.S. GSA Fine Arts Collection**  
  • *Countryside* (1939, color woodcut)  
  • *Apples & Tubules* (1937, color woodcut)  
  • *El Andaluz* (1936, color woodcut)

- The **youngest** of these is ***Countryside* (1939)**.

- According to the GSA’s own loan‑record database, the **westernmost museum that currently holds this work** is the **San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA)** in San Francisco, California.
